tagline: Ancient pyramids, chilies and two coasts
overview:
Mexico stretches from the United States border south to Guatemala and Belize, a country about three times the size of Texas with long coasts on both the Pacific Ocean and the Gulf of Mexico. It narrows in the south at the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, then hooks east into the flat limestone Yucatán Peninsula. Mexico City, the capital, sits in a high valley about 2,240 meters up and anchors one of the largest urban areas in the world.

About 130 million people live in Mexico, more than in any other Spanish-speaking country. Spanish is the national language, and some 70 Indigenous languages, including Nahuatl, Maya and Zapotec, are recognized and spoken by millions of people. Mexico is a federal republic of 31 states plus the capital. Mexican cooking, from tacos and tamales to slow-simmered mole, is listed by UNESCO as cultural heritage, and Mexican music, murals, films and writers are known around the world.
landAndNature: Two great mountain chains, the Sierra Madre Occidental and the Sierra Madre Oriental, run down either side of the country, with a high plateau between them and a belt of volcanoes crossing the middle; Pico de Orizaba reaches 5,636 meters, and Popocatépetl still puffs smoke near the capital. Northern deserts hold giant cardón cacti and roadrunners, while southern states are covered in rainforest with jaguars, howler monkeys and toucans. The Yucatán has no surface rivers at all, and rain drains into cenotes, deep water-filled sinkholes in the limestone. Each autumn millions of monarch butterflies arrive from Canada and cluster on fir trees in Michoacán.
peopleAndCulture: Corn is the foundation of Mexican cooking, ground into tortillas eaten at nearly every meal, and roughly 60 kinds of chili add heat and flavor to everything from fresh salsa to dark, chocolate-rich mole sauce. Day of the Dead on November 1 and 2 brings families to cemeteries with marigolds, sugar skulls and candles to remember relatives; it is a celebration rather than a day of mourning. Mariachi bands in silver-studded suits play at parties, and lucha libre wrestlers fight in bright masks. Soccer fills stadiums, and artists such as Frida Kahlo and the muralist Diego Rivera are known everywhere.
history: Great civilizations rose here thousands of years ago: the Olmec carved colossal stone heads, the Maya built stepped pyramids and tracked the stars with remarkable precision, and the Aztecs founded Tenochtitlan on a lake island in 1325, growing it into one of the largest cities on Earth. Spanish forces under Hernán Cortés, joined by Indigenous allies and helped by diseases that killed enormous numbers of people, took the Aztec capital in 1521, and Spain ruled for three centuries. Mexico won independence in 1821, lost half its territory to the United States in a war ending in 1848, and passed through a revolution from 1910 to 1920 that reshaped land ownership and politics.
funFacts: Mexico City is sinking, dropping tens of centimeters a year in places because it was built on a drained lake bed.
Chocolate, chili, corn, tomatoes, avocados and vanilla were all first grown in Mexico before spreading worldwide.
Monarch butterflies fly thousands of kilometers from Canada to a handful of Mexican forests where they gather each winter.
At Chichen Itza the main pyramid is built so that a shadow shaped like a snake slides down its steps at the equinox.
Mexico has more UNESCO World Heritage sites than any other country in the Americas.
The volcano rabbit, one of the smallest rabbits on Earth, lives only on volcano slopes near Mexico City.
